name: Idaho

sales.rateNote: Idaho's sales tax rate is 6% and its use tax rate is also 6% (Idaho State Tax Commission, Sales and Use Taxes: Basics Guide). Some resort cities add a voter-approved local option tax.

local.levies: resort cities with a voter-approved local option sales tax (23 listed by the Tax Commission, such as Ketchum, McCall, Sandpoint and Sun Valley), and auditorium districts
local.capNote: Resort cities choose what they tax: some tax everything subject to the state tax, others only lodging, alcohol by the drink and restaurant food.

groceries.note: Food is taxed at the general 6% rate; Idaho returns part of it through the food tax credit (formerly the grocery tax credit) on the income tax return: $155 per resident and per qualifying dependent for 2025, or up to $250 with receipts for residents who are not required to file.

clothing.note: No clothing exemption: sales tax applies to every retail sale of goods unless an exemption applies.

prescriptionDrugs.note: Drugs and listed medical products are exempt when bought by a patient with a practitioner's prescription (Idaho Code 63-3622N).

useTax.note: Use tax is due on goods used or stored in Idaho when the buyer did not pay at least 6% sales tax, including online and out-of-state purchases; Idaho adopted sales and use tax in 1965 and credits sales tax paid to another state.

facts.text: Idaho adopted its sales tax and use tax in 1965.
Short-term rentals of 30 days or less, meals and drinks, admissions and digital books, videos, music or games bought with a permanent right of use are taxable sales.
Separately stated shipping to the buyer, installation labor and repair labor are not part of the taxable price; parts used in repairs are taxable.
A trade-in allowance reduces the taxable price: an $800 range with a $250 trade-in is taxed on $550.
For tax year 2024, more than 101,000 residents who were not required to file a return claimed a refund of sales tax paid on food.

property.levied: Local taxing districts (counties, cities, school, highway and other special districts) levy property tax on net taxable value; county assessors value property and county treasurers collect.

assessment.text: All taxable property is assessed at 100% of current market value as of January 1, less statutory exemptions such as the homeowner's exemption. Each taxing district can raise its property tax budget by only 3% a year, plus revenue from new construction and annexation, unless voters approve more.

homestead.name: Homeowner's Exemption
homestead.text: Reduces the net taxable value of an owner-occupied primary residence and up to one acre of land by half, up to a maximum reduction of $125,000 (fixed since 2021 until the legislature changes it).
homestead.applyBy: Apply to the county assessor by April 15 for the exemption to apply that year; it then renews automatically while the owner qualifies.

otherRelief.name: Property Tax Reduction (Circuit Breaker)
otherRelief.text: Reduces property tax on the primary home and up to one acre by up to $1,500 for qualifying owners (seniors, disabled, certain veterans, etc.) with prior-year household income of $39,130 or less after deductions; apply every year between January 1 and April 15. Since tax year 2022 the home's exemption-eligible value must be below 200% of the county median.

dueDates.text: Two installments: first half due by December 20 and second half by June 20. A 2% late charge applies to an unpaid half, plus 12% annual interest counted from January 1.

facts.text: The homeowner's exemption halves the taxable value of a primary residence, capped at a $125,000 reduction since 2021.
Before 2021 the maximum homeowner's exemption was indexed each year to the Idaho house price index; it was $100,000 the year before it moved to $125,000.
Each taxing district's property tax budget can grow by only 3% a year plus new construction and annexation, unless voters approve bonds or overrides.
The Circuit Breaker can cut a qualifying owner's property tax by up to $1,500 and must be re-applied for every year by April 15.
Property taxes are paid in two halves, due December 20 and June 20.

uncertain: Property facts come from the Canyon County Assessor and Treasurer (official county government site) describing statewide Idaho rules; the $39,130 circuit-breaker income limit is the figure shown there for the current cycle and is indexed. Due dates (December 20 / June 20) are statewide in Idaho Code but were read on the Canyon County page.
Property tax relief changes from the 2025-2026 legislative sessions could not be checked on the Idaho Legislature or Tax Commission sites.
